clue.text: Aware of two men down

parts.note: K and N are the king and knight, two chessmen
being down means owing, short of money or points

explanation.surface: Someone realises that two men have been knocked over or are feeling low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Men' are chess pieces here: king K and knight N. 'Down' in the sense of out of pocket gives OWING.
explanation.definitionFit: A knowing look is one that shows the person is already informed and conscious of something.

clue.text: Hotline fails, something from the Stone Age

indicators.note: a line that fails is broken, so the letters of the word before it break apart and regroup

explanation.surface: A telephone hotline breaks down, as primitive as a relic of prehistory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fails' rearranges the letters of HOTLINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A neolith is a stone tool or object made in the New Stone Age.

clue.text: Shrink from cold, tucking into some alcohol

indicators.note: one piece is tucked inside another, here the letter for cold going into the drink

parts.note: wine is a kind of alcohol
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: Someone recoils from the cold while enjoying a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking into' puts C inside WINE.
explanation.definitionFit: To wince is to flinch or recoil, drawing back in pain or distaste.

clue.text: They are missing food with pained expressions

parts.note: nosh is informal British slang for food
'ow' is what people say when hurt, so OWS are cries of pain

explanation.surface: Diners are absent, leaving their food and grimacing faces behind.
explanation.definitionFit: No-shows are people who book or are expected but fail to turn up.

clue.text: Programme on TV that may support the Speaker

parts.note: a soap is a soap opera, a television programme
the box is informal British slang for the television set

explanation.surface: A television show might back up the Speaker of the House of Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Speaker' suggests the chair of Parliament but means any public orator.
explanation.definitionFit: A soapbox is a crate a street orator stands on to address a crowd, so it holds up whoever is talking.

clue.text: Youngster to switch positions over in place for drill

indicators.note: turned over, so the letters of the whole wordplay are read backwards

parts.note: a girl is a youngster
a power switch is marked I for on and O for off

explanation.surface: A child is told to swap places in readiness for a practice drill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses GIRLIO. The I and O symbols on appliance switches are the two positions.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil rig is the platform from which wells are bored into the seabed.

clue.text: Advantage for us sporting baggy clothes

parts.note: a plus is an advantage or benefit

indicators.note: sporting suggests playing about, so the two words beside it are jumbled

explanation.surface: We gain an edge by wearing loose-fitting sportswear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sporting' rearranges FORUS into FOURS.
explanation.definitionFit: Plus fours are loose knickerbockers gathered below the knee, traditionally worn for golf.

clue.text: One third of trimester with head away, I get busy

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which is taken away

parts.note: a trimester is three months, so a third of it is a month
the ego is the self, the I

explanation.surface: A pregnant woman, a third through her trimester and her mind elsewhere, keeps active.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with head away' drops the M of MONTH to leave ONTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the go is constantly active and occupied.

clue.text: IoW feature last visited by people making maps of course

parts.note: the Needles are chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight

indicators.note: a place visited has someone coming into it, so the mapmakers go inside the word for last

parts.note: to last is to stay or endure
OS is the Ordnance Survey, Britain's national mapping agency

explanation.surface: The cartographers visit the Isle of Wight's famous rocks last on their route.
explanation.walkthrough: IoW is the Isle of Wight, an island off England's south coast; 'visited by' is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Needless to say is a set phrase meaning obviously, as anyone would expect.

clue.text: Cut complaint that's expressed

indicators.note: something expressed is spoken out, so the word for complaint is heard rather than read

parts.note: a moan is a complaint

explanation.surface: A grumble about a cut is voiced.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent MOAN and MOWN sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Grass that has been mown has been trimmed with a mower.

clue.text: Hustling, sell us this leisurewear

indicators.note: hustling means jostling or pushing about, so the letters are shoved into a new order

explanation.surface: A pushy salesman tries to sell us some casual clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hustling' rearranges SELLUSTHIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Shell suits are shiny nylon tracksuits popular as casual wear in the 1980s and 90s.

clue.text: Old Roman company employing decorator

indicators.note: a firm employing someone takes them in, so the decorator goes inside the company

parts.note: an icer decorates cakes

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman firm takes on a painter-decorator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employing' signals containment; the decorator works on cakes, not walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero was a Roman statesman and orator of the first century BC.

clue.text: In small segments, give out last message — fine, in fact

indicators.note: the second 'in' places the message and the fine within the word for fact

parts.note: in deed and in fact both mean actually, so deed stands for fact
RIP, rest in peace, is the final message on a gravestone
F is the abbreviation for fine on pencil leads

explanation.surface: Someone eking out a final message insists it is in fact fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts RIPF inside DEED.
explanation.definitionFit: To drip-feed is to supply something gradually in small amounts, like a medical drip.

clue.text: Those fools are all ordinary people

parts.note: 'them' is colloquial for those, as in 'them boots'
asses are fools

explanation.surface: A snob dismisses the general public as idiots.
explanation.definitionFit: The masses are the common people, the bulk of the population.

clue.text: Old American people get bigger: why not?

parts.note: the Maya are a pre-Columbian people of Central America
to swell is to grow larger

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs at the idea of an ancient civilisation growing.
explanation.definitionFit: May as well expresses mild agreement, like shrugging that nothing stops it.

clue.text: Credit turning round anti-British slogan

indicators.note: the slogan is turned round, so its letters are read in reverse

parts.note: 'Sod UK' would be a slogan hostile to Britain; sod is a British curse

explanation.surface: Praise is reversed by a protest chant against Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning round' reverses SOD UK.
explanation.definitionFit: Kudos is prestige or praise earned for an achievement.

clue.text: Virginia houses some titled uncle

indicators.note: a place that houses something holds it inside, so the state abbreviation contains the word for some

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for the US state of Virginia
any can mean some, as in 'have you any?'

explanation.surface: A US state is home to a relative with an aristocratic title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'titled' suggests nobility but means named in a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Vanya is Chekhov's play, so its uncle appears in the name of the work.

clue.text: Musical film shot in Oz

indicators.note: the filming happened in Australia, so the word for shot sits inside it

parts.note: Oz is slang for Australia, abbreviated AUS
a film that has been shot has been made

explanation.surface: A film with music was shot on location in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals containment, and the inserted word splits the abbreviation after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Amadeus is the 1984 film about Mozart, full of his music.

clue.text: Showing hammering: it's 7-0

indicators.note: a hammering batters something out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: seven and nought, with the zero read as the letter O

explanation.surface: A sports report notes that a seven-nil drubbing speaks for itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hammering' rearranges ITS plus SEVEN and O. The scoreline sounds like a result, but 'hammering' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostensive means demonstrating directly, defining a thing by pointing it out.

clue.text: Tragic figure not heading to French city in initial stages

indicators.note: without its head, so the first letter of the word is lost

parts.note: King Lear is the hero of Shakespeare's tragedy
Lyon is a city in France

explanation.surface: A tragic hero avoids travelling to a French city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not heading' drops the L of LEAR to leave EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Early on means near the beginning of a process or period.

clue.text: Dislike not having a translation

indicators.note: the word lacks the letter that follows, so it is removed

parts.note: an aversion is a strong dislike

explanation.surface: Someone dislikes being without a translation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not having' removes A from AVERSION.
explanation.definitionFit: A version of a text can mean a rendering of it in another language.

clue.text: With trouble, wife has endless long piece to iron

definitions.note: in Cockney rhyming slang 'trouble and strife' means wife, so with trouble the answer makes wife

indicators.note: without an end, so the last letter of the word goes

parts.note: a strip is a long narrow piece
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A troubled wife has an unending length of cloth to press.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang swaps a word for a rhyming phrase: 'trouble and strife' is wife. 'endless' cuts the P from STRIP.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyming slang phrase pairs trouble with this word to mean a man's spouse.

clue.text: Not one to lose argument, raised voice

indicators.note: not having the following word, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: to fail is to lose, not succeed
I is the Roman numeral for one
a set-to is a quarrel or argument

explanation.surface: A sore loser who never concedes a debate ends up shouting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' removes I (one) from FAIL to leave FAL. 'raised voice' suggests shouting but means pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Falsetto is a male singing voice pitched artificially high, above the natural range.

clue.text: Promising to hold retreat, initially after a series of prayers

indicators.note: the outer word holds the others inside it

parts.note: a rosy future is a promising one

indicators.note: the first letter of retreat comes after A in the charade
initially points to the first letter of the word retreat

explanation.surface: A hopeful worshipper goes on retreat for a set of devotions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hold' puts AR inside ROSY.
explanation.definitionFit: The rosary is a sequence of Catholic prayers counted on beads.

clue.text: Black book central to special offer

indicators.note: the book is put at the centre of the offer

parts.note: a sale is a period of special offers

explanation.surface: A black book is the centrepiece of a shop promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central to' puts B inside SALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sable is the heraldic name for black, and also poetic for dark.

clue.text: Some peers are at this place, a dirty mess

parts.note: here means at this place

indicators.note: a mess is a jumble, so the letters are muddled up

explanation.surface: Some lords find their surroundings filthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' rearranges ADIRTY into DITARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereditary peers inherit their House of Lords titles rather than being appointed to them.

clue.text: Run aboard huge vessel

indicators.note: on board means inside the vessel, so the letter goes inside the word

parts.note: big means huge
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone sprints across the deck of an enormous ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aboard' puts R inside BIG.
explanation.definitionFit: A brig is a two-masted square-rigged sailing ship.

clue.text: A belated idea to edit book of David's songs

parts.note: a PS, or postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter
to alter is to edit or change

explanation.surface: An afterthought prompts revision of King David's hymnbook.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalter is the Book of Psalms, traditionally attributed to King David.

clue.text: Fire out of control? Suppose not

parts.note: to infer is to deduce or suppose
no can mean not, as in 'no better'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a blaze is raging and is told they assume wrongly.
explanation.definitionFit: An inferno is a large, raging and uncontrollable blaze.
